title: How Do Organisms Respond When Environments Change?

figure.label: 📷 Real photos · The same lake, 22 years apart

opener.title: How Do Organisms Respond When Environments Change?
opener.question: When an environment changes, why do some organisms survive while others don't?

k-warmup.text: One winter night in eighteen ninety-eight, a storm knocked one hundred thirty-six sparrows out of the sky. Slide the handle to guess how many woke up. Then tap the one thing you think decided it, save your guess, and write why below.

k-part1.text: This is the real lecture, printed in eighteen ninety-nine. A scientist named Bumpus measured every single bird from that storm. Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English, then find the two hunt lines.

k-quiz.text: Three quick questions, just for you. They are not graded. Tap an answer and read the note under it. Think about the three ways organisms can respond.

k-assign.text: Now write your half of page twenty-one. Answer the two Part B questions. In Part C, make your survivor evidence card. Then tap evidence cards in the planner and build your C-E-R about how a species gets through change.

k-words.text: Environment. Change. Survive. Variation. Migrate. Adaptation.

wordlens.intro: Tap a word to see what it means.

words.def: Everything around a living thing: temperature, water, food, and the other living things nearby.
When something becomes different. Environments can change fast, like a storm, or slowly, like a warming climate.
To stay alive through hard conditions, long enough to have young.
Small differences between individuals of the same species. One sparrow may be a little lighter than another.
To move to a new place. Many birds migrate south in winter to find food.
A trait that helps an organism survive in its environment. It can be a body part or a behavior.

tray.title: The night of the sparrows
tray.intro: February 1, 1898. An ice storm batters Providence, Rhode Island. In the morning, 136 stunned house sparrows are carried into a university laboratory. Some will wake up. Some won't.
job: Slide the handle: how many of the 136 wake up?
Tap the ONE thing you think decided it.
Save your guess, then write why.
tray.photoAlt: A row of house sparrows crowded together on a snowy stone ledge.
tray.photoCap: House sparrows riding out a snowfall. Photo: Andrey (CC BY 2.0).
tray.trayAlt: A tray of 136 small bird marks. The marks you choose light up to show your guess of how many sparrows revived.

facts.label: Size: the biggest, heaviest birds made it
Build: birds with the right body made it
Luck: it could have been anyone
Age: only older, experienced birds made it

tray.notYet: Set your number and pick one factor, then save.
tray.saved: 🔒 Saved: {n} of 136 wake up, and {f} decided it. Part 4 checks your guess against the scientist's real count.
tray.reasonPrompt: Why do you think so? Write at least 2 sentences. What would help a small bird live through an ice storm?
tray.placeholder: I think about ___ birds wake up because… I picked ___ because…

source.title: The scientist who measured every bird
source.alt: Two printed pages in English from an 1899 science lecture. The left page, 209, introduces the sparrow storm. The right page, 217, states the lecture's main conclusion in slanted type.
source.intro: The sparrows were carried into Brown University, where a scientist named Hermon Bumpus worked. Bumpus saw a once-in-a-lifetime chance: he measured every one of the 136 birds, the living and the dead, and asked the storm a question no one had asked it before. A year later he printed what he found.
job: Tap each yellow line to read it in plain English.
Then find the two lines in the hunts.

lines.en: The title: The Elimination of the Unfit, as Illustrated by the Introduced Sparrow. 'Eliminated' means removed. 'Unfit' means not matched to the conditions, like a key that doesn't fit a lock.
Bumpus starts with a warning: scientists talk about natural selection all the time, but almost no one has ever caught it in the act. Real examples, he says, are very rare.
On February 1 of this year, 1898, after an uncommonly severe storm of snow, rain, and sleet, a number of English sparrows were brought to the Anatomical Laboratory of Brown University.
Seventy-two of these birds revived. Sixty-four perished. ('Revived' means woke up. 'Perished' means died.)

The purpose of this lecture is to show that the birds which perished, perished not through accident, but because they were physically disqualified. And the birds which survived, survived because of their physical characters.

His conclusion, in slanted type: Natural selection is most destructive of those birds which have departed most from the ideal type. In plain words: the birds built furthest from 'just right' were the ones the storm removed.
Among the 72 survivors, 23 birds had at least one unusual measurement, but almost all of them had only one. Among the 64 that died, several had four, five, even six unusual features.
Of the 136 birds, five even had albino feathers: white feathers where brown ones should be. Variation shows up everywhere, even in color.

asks.q: Hunt 1: Find the line that tells how many birds woke up and how many died.
asks.yes: Yes: 72 revived, 64 perished. Keep your Warm-Up guess in mind. Part 4 compares it.
asks.no: Not that one. Look near the bottom of the left page.

asks.q: Hunt 2: Find the line where Bumpus says the deaths were NOT an accident.
asks.yes: Yes. That one sentence is the whole lecture: who lived and who died was decided by the birds' bodies, not by chance. Next you'll see what decided it in a pond.
asks.no: Close. It's on the left page, right after the counts.

source.credit: Source: Hermon C. Bumpus, 'The Elimination of the Unfit as Illustrated by the Introduced Sparrow', Biological Lectures from the Marine Biological Laboratory, Wood's Hole, 1898 session (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1899), pages 209 and 217. Scan from the Internet Archive (public domain). Plain-English version written for this lesson.

winter.kicker: Part 2 game · Three ways to respond
winter.title: Run the winter
winter.intro: Deep winter is coming to one northern pond. Here are six organisms that live there. Every one of them must answer the cold somehow.
job: For each organism, tap the response you think it uses.
Choose for all six, then tap Run the winter.
Read what really happens to each one.

cards.name: Black bear
cards.alt: Two black bears curled up asleep in the snow.
cards.clue: All fall it ate and ate, and now it carries a thick layer of fat.
cards.why: It stays and copes: the bear dens up and sleeps through the worst of winter, living off its stored fat. Its heart slows from about 50 beats a minute to about 10.
cards.hint: A bear can't fly south, and bears don't die off every winter. What does all that stored fat make possible?

cards.name: Canada goose
cards.alt: A V of Canada geese flying across a blue sky.
cards.clue: Strong wings, and the whole flock is restless.
cards.why: It moves: the flock migrates south to open water and food, and returns in spring. Geese fly in a V to save energy on the trip.
cards.hint: Those wings can carry it hundreds of kilometers. Does it need to stay at all?

cards.name: Red fox
cards.alt: A red fox with a thick orange winter coat standing in deep snow.
cards.clue: Its summer coat has been growing thicker for weeks.
cards.why: It stays and copes: a dense winter coat keeps it warm, and it hunts right through the cold. It can even hear mice moving under the snow.
cards.hint: Foxes don't migrate. Look at what its body grew for this exact season.

cards.name: Sugar maple
cards.alt: A sugar maple tree glowing yellow in fall, dropping its leaves.
cards.clue: A tree can't walk. Its leaves are already turning.
cards.why: It stays and copes: the maple drops every leaf and shuts down for winter. Leaves lose water, and a tree can't drink from frozen ground, so bare branches are the safe move.
cards.hint: It can't move, and it won't die: sugar maples live hundreds of years. What is it doing with those leaves?

cards.name: Wood frog
cards.alt: A brown wood frog with a dark eye mask sitting on a rock.
cards.clue: Too small to travel. It crawls under the leaf litter instead.
cards.why: It stays and copes, in the strangest way in the forest: the wood frog freezes almost solid. Its heart stops for weeks. In spring it thaws out and hops away.
cards.hint: It sounds impossible, but this frog does survive, right where it is.

cards.name: Bluegill in a shallow pond
cards.alt: A bluegill, a flat round fish with an orange chest, swimming.
cards.clue: Its pond is small and shallow, and thick ice is sealing it over.
cards.why: Many can't cope. Under thick ice and snow, pond plants stop making oxygen. In a very shallow pond the oxygen can run out before spring, and many fish don't make it. Scientists call it winterkill.
cards.hint: The fish can't leave the pond, and it can't breathe air. What happens if the oxygen under the ice runs out?

winter.pickAll: Choose a response for all 6 organisms, then run the winter.
winter.win: Three responses (move away, stay and cope, can't cope), but six different ways to live them. And notice: the goose's answer is useless to the fish. Each organism can only use the body and behaviors it already has.
winter.againLabel: ↺ Clear my choices and try again
winter.credit: Photos: sleeping black bears, ForestWander.com (CC BY-SA 3.0 US); Canada geese, John Benson (CC BY 2.0); red fox, St Clair Macaulay (CC BY 3.0); sugar maple, James St. John (CC BY 2.0); wood frog, Jasper Shide (CC0); bluegill, Ltshears (public domain).

band.kicker: Part 3 game · Variation is the backup plan
band.title: Three winters
band.intro: Here is a model flock of 10 sparrows, lined up from lightest to heaviest, like the real birds Bumpus weighed (his sparrows ran from about 23 to 31 grams). You are the storm.
job: Drag the two handles to choose which sparrows survive this winter.
Tap Next winter and watch the new flock hatch.
Do it three times. Then answer the question.
band.model: The sparrows are drawings, and this is a model: real storms don't pick a neat band. But real survivors do have the chicks.
band.bandLine: Survivors this winter: {a} to {b} grams ({n} of 10 birds)
band.needSome: At least two sparrows must survive, or there is no next generation at all.
band.chicksLine: The {n} survivors had chicks. Most chicks are built like their parents.
band.endLine: After three winters, your flock looks different. Compare the first row with the last.
band.ask: Did any single sparrow change its own body?

opts.t: No. Each bird kept the body it hatched with. The MIX of birds changed
Yes. The birds grew new bodies on purpose to survive
opts.hint: Look at any one bird in your rows. It never changes. Only who survives, and who has chicks, changes.

band.win: Right. No bird can change its own build, and no bird chooses its traits. But when the environment removes some and spares others, the whole population shifts. That is why variation is a species' backup plan.
band.mis: A squirrel can't grow thicker fur because it wants to. But a squirrel POPULATION can end up with thicker fur over many generations, because the thick-furred ones keep surviving the cold. You just made that happen with sparrows.

drain.cardIntro: A hot, dry summer settles in, and a small pond starts to disappear. Five organisms live here. You control the water.
drain.title: Who makes it when the pond dries up?
drain.intro: Drag the water level down, slowly. Each time the water drops far enough, watch what one of the organisms does. Then tag its response.
job: Drag the water down and watch each organism act.
Tag each one: Move away, Stay and cope, or Can't cope.
Fill the whole table, then bring the rain back.
drain.pondAlt: A small green pond ringed with cattails, with the water level you control drawn across it.
drain.mudAlt: Dry, cracked mud where the pond used to be.
drain.stageModel: Real photos, model pond: the blue water line is drawn, and you are speeding up weeks of drought.

orgs.name: Duck
orgs.alt: A mallard duck with wings spread, taking off.
orgs.act: The water drops. The duck circles once, then flies to a lake ten miles away.
orgs.why: Move away. Wings make the duck's answer easy: it simply leaves.
orgs.hint: It flew ten miles. Is that staying?
orgs.did: Flew to a lake ten miles away

orgs.name: Frog
orgs.alt: A green and brown leopard frog sitting on wet sand.
orgs.act: The shallows turn to mud. The frog buries itself and slows its body way, way down.
orgs.why: Stay and cope. Buried in damp mud with its body nearly switched off, the frog can wait out the drought.
orgs.hint: It didn't leave, and it isn't dead. It's waiting.
orgs.did: Buried itself in the mud and slowed its body down

orgs.name: Turtle
orgs.alt: A painted turtle walking through plants at the pond edge.
orgs.act: The pond is half gone. The turtle digs into the soft bottom and goes still until rain returns.
orgs.why: Stay and cope. Dug into the mud, nearly motionless, the turtle barely needs food, water, or air.
orgs.hint: Digging in and going still is a way of riding it out.
orgs.did: Dug into the soft bottom and went still

orgs.name: Cattail
orgs.alt: Cattails with brown seed heads at the edge of the water.
orgs.act: The cattail's leaves turn brown and die back, but its thick underground stems stay alive in the damp mud.
orgs.why: Stay and cope. The green top is sacrificed; the living underground stems wait for rain, ready to sprout.
orgs.hint: The leaves died, but is the PLANT dead? Look underground.
orgs.did: Leaves died back; underground stems stayed alive

orgs.name: Fish
orgs.alt: A bluegill, a flat round fish with an orange chest.
orgs.act: Only a warm, muddy puddle is left. The fish can't leave the water, and many of them die.
orgs.why: Many can't cope. A fish can't cross dry land and can't wait in mud. When the last water goes, most fish go with it.
orgs.hint: Every other organism had an escape or a waiting trick. Does the fish have either?
orgs.did: Couldn't leave the water; many died

drain.tagFirst: Lower the water until an organism acts, then tag it.
drain.rainQ: The pond refills. Which organism is first to grow back from INSIDE the dried pond?

rainOpts.t: The cattail: its living underground stems are already there, ready to sprout
The fish: they come back as soon as the water does
rainOpts.hint: The fish that died can't return. New fish have to arrive from somewhere else, like eggs stuck to a duck's feet or a flood from another pond. That takes much longer.

rainOpts.t: The duck: it flies back the same day
rainOpts.hint: True, the duck returns fast, but it comes back from OUTSIDE. The question asks what grows back from inside the dried pond.

drain.varQ: One more look. Not all frogs dig equally well. If the drought ran LONGER, which frogs would make it?

varOpts.t: The frogs that can dig a little deeper, where the mud stays damp
All the frogs equally, because they're all frogs
varOpts.hint: They're all frogs, but they are not all the same. That's variation. Remember the sparrows.

drain.varWin: Right. Variation again: same species, different diggers, different chances. The deep diggers' tadpoles inherit deep-digging parents.
drain.claimLine: 📋 For your CER: when a pond dries up, organisms that can MOVE AWAY or WAIT IT OUT are most likely to survive. And even within one species, some individuals are better equipped than others.
drain.credit: Photos: pond, Diane9247 (CC BY-SA 3.0); cracked mud, Andrew Cattoir, Lake Mead NRA (public domain); mallard, Bert de Tilly (CC BY-SA 4.0); southern leopard frog, Judy Gallagher (CC BY 2.0); painted turtle, Sixflashphoto (CC BY-SA 4.0); cattails, Thomas Metaxas (CC BY-SA 4.0); bluegill, Ltshears (public domain).

reveal.title: Now check your Warm-Up guess
reveal.realFact: Their build. The survivors were a little SHORTER and LIGHTER, with longer wing bones and longer legs. Not luck, and not size.

twist.head: Even the scientist guessed wrong.
twist.line: Bumpus wrote that he would have picked the big, heavy birds to survive, 'unhesitatingly.' Then he weighed them. The birds that died averaged 25.8 grams. The survivors averaged 25.2. His own numbers proved his guess wrong.
twist.chain: That is why scientists measure instead of assuming. Tomorrow, you'll read survival numbers the same way Bumpus did, for finches on a tiny island hit by drought.

footage.title: A lake disappears in 40 years
footage.intro: NASA's Landsat satellites photographed Lake Mead, the biggest reservoir in the United States, every year from 1985 to 2025. Here are those 40 years in 15 seconds.
look: Watch the lake's arms get thinner, year by year.
A drought this slow is still an environmental change. Who has to respond?
Fish, herons, bighorn sheep and cattails all live here. Which of the three responses is open to each?
footage.credit: Video: 'Lake Mead Recedes', NASA Scientific Visualization Studio / Landsat (public domain). Slowed and resized for this lesson.

data.title: The Arctic's summer ice, measured for 46 years
data.intro: Every September, satellites measure how much of the Arctic Ocean is still covered by ice at summer's end. Polar bears hunt from that ice. Here is every September from 1979 to 2024.
job: Drag across the line to read each year.
Compare the first ten years with the last ten.
data.ask: Find the lowest point on the whole line. Which year is it?

opts.t: 2012: about 3.6 million square kilometers, less than half the 1980 amount

opts.hint: Drag to the far left. 1979 is one of the HIGHEST points, at about 7 million.
2024 is low, about 4.4. But drag to 2012 and read the number there.

data.win: Right: September 2012, about 3.6 million square kilometers. This is a slow change, like the shrinking lake at the top of this lesson. The animals that live on the ice are answering it right now, with the same three responses you tagged in the pond.
data.alt: A line graph of September Arctic sea ice from 1979 to 2024. The line wiggles but falls from about 7 million square kilometers in the 1980s to between 4 and 5 million in the 2020s, with the lowest point, 3.57, in 2012.
data.credit: Data: September monthly average Arctic sea ice extent, NSIDC Sea Ice Index version 3 (1979 to 2019 via NOAA Climate.gov; 2020 to 2024 from NSIDC's monthly reports). Downloaded 25 Nov 2026.

cabinet.title: A giant that didn't make it
cabinet.alt: A 3D scan of a mounted woolly mammoth skeleton with long, curved tusks.
cabinet.text: This is a 3D scan of a woolly mammoth skeleton from the Smithsonian. Woolly mammoths stood about 3 meters tall at the shoulder and were built for the Ice Age: thick fur, small ears, and a hump of stored fat. Then the world warmed, their cold grasslands shrank, and human hunters spread. Mammoths disappeared from the mainland about 10,000 years ago. The last small herd lived on an Arctic island until about 4,000 years ago. 'Can't cope' is a real ending, even for giants.
cabinet.credit: 3D model: Mammuthus primigenius (Blumenbach), Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History. CC0.

boxes.label: Three ways to respond
boxes.prompt: From the drying pond: name one organism that moved away, one that stayed and coped, and one that couldn't cope. One sentence each.

chain.what: Where does a tree come from?
Can a plant fix the air?
How do we draw the path of energy?
Where does all that blood go?
Why does a giant need fat bones?
Why do finches have different beaks?
Who survives when the storm comes?
What do the survival numbers say?

planner.title: Plan before you write
planner.intro: Tap two or more pieces of evidence to add them to your Evidence box. Then write your claim and reasoning in your own words.
cards: In the 1898 storm, 72 of 136 sparrows revived and 64 perished. Bumpus showed the difference was in their bodies, not luck.
The sparrows that died were, on average, a little longer and heavier than the ones that lived. Even the scientist had guessed wrong.
In the drying pond, the duck flew away, the turtle and frog dug in, and the cattail's underground stems survived. But many fish died.
In the winter pond, the goose left, the bear slept off its fat, and the wood frog froze nearly solid. In shallow water, some bluegill didn't make it.
Some frogs can dig deeper than others. The same species, different individuals, different chances.
In the three-winters model, no sparrow ever changed its own body. But the flock changed, because the survivors had the chicks.
